warmup.q: Six nodes sit on a hash ring with one token each, at random positions. Roughly how much of the ring does the luckiest node own?
options: 16.7%, a sixth: hashing spreads things evenly
About 20%: random positions come out close to even
About 40%: random points leave some very long gaps
It depends on how many keys you store
warmup.why: Hashing spreads many keys evenly, but six node positions are only six random points, and six random cuts of a circle are very uneven. With S nodes the longest arc is on average (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/S) / S of the ring, about 41% for six. The ring demo in the Data models track's first lesson got 44.6%. The share is a property of the ring, not of the keys.

sections.h: One token per node gives some nodes far more than their share
sections.html:
Lesson 1 hashed each partition key and picked a shard with hash mod N. That spreads keys evenly until N changes. The Data models track's first lesson counted the damage: going from 4 nodes to 5 moves 80% of the keys, because the remainders mod 4 and mod 5 agree for only 4 numbers in every 20. (This lesson writes S for the number of nodes, because N is taken: Dynamo uses it for the number of copies.)

Consistent hashing is the fix that Dynamo and Cassandra are built on. Lay every possible hash value around a circle, the ring. Each node sits at the hash of its name; that position is its token. Each key sits at the hash of the key and belongs to the first node you meet walking clockwise. A node owns the arc that ends at its own token. A new node takes only the keys on the arc just before its token, from one neighbour, and no other key moves. That's the "consistent" in the name: most of the assignment stays put when the set of nodes changes. It has nothing to do with consistent data.

The ring has a flaw of its own. The ring demo in that same first lesson put six nodes on an MD5 ring with one token each, and node-E ended up owning 44.6% of the ring while node-D owned 5%. That wasn't bad luck. It's what one random position per node does.

Hashes are as good as random, and random points on a circle don't spread out evenly. They clump in some places and leave long gaps in others. With S nodes, the longest gap is on average (1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/S) / S of the ring. For six nodes that's about 41%, where the fair share is 16.7%. The node at the end of that gap holds 41% of the keys, stores 41% of the data and serves 41% of the requests, while its neighbour idles. Buying a seventh machine doesn't fix it: the new token lands at random too.

It gets worse when nodes come and go. A node that joins takes whatever arc its token lands in, all of it from one neighbour. A node that dies hands its whole arc to the next node clockwise, which can double that node's load at the worst moment. Dynamo's paper names the problem in section 4.2, "non-uniform data and load distribution", and a second one: one token per node can't say that one machine is bigger than another.

Version 2 gives every physical node many tokens. Dynamo calls them virtual nodes. Node A takes T tokens, at the hashes of node-A#0, node-A#1 and so on, and owns T small arcs scattered round the ring. Its share is the sum of those arcs, and a sum of many random pieces lands much closer to its average than one piece does. The demo below measures six nodes. With one token each, the biggest share is 44.0%; with 64 it's 18.6%, and with 256 it's 17.4%, against a fair 16.7%.

The improvement isn't smooth. Sixteen random tokens still leave one node at 24.3%, worse than four did. Random placement is noisy when T is small, which is why Cassandra doesn't place its 16 tokens at random (section 3). Tokens also fix the second problem: give a machine twice the capacity twice the tokens.

Each node owns many small arcs scattered round one ring, and a key belongs to the arc it lands in. Joining, leaving, copies and hot keys below are all questions about those arcs.

try.title: Measure the shares with 1 to 256 tokens per node
steps: Read RingBalanceDemo.kt. It builds the ring as a TreeMap from token to node, with T tokens per node at the MD5 of node-A#0, node-A#1, ..., and sums the arc before each token. No Docker needed.
Predict: with 16 tokens per node, will the largest share be closer to 44% or to the fair 16.7%?

code.title: RingBalanceDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l02.demo import java.nio.ByteBuffer import java.security.MessageDigest import java.util.TreeMap /** Where text lands on a ring of 2^64 positions: the first 8 bytes of its MD5. */ fun position(text: String): Long = ByteBuffer.wrap(MessageDigest.getInstance("MD5").digest(text.toByteArray())).long /** A ring with [tokensPerNode] tokens for each node: token position -> node. */ fun ring(nodes: List<String>, tokensPerNode: Int): TreeMap<Long, String> { val tokens = TreeMap<Long, String>() for (node in nodes) for (i in 0 until tokensPerNode) tokens[position("$node#$i")] = node return tokens } /** Each node's share of the ring: the gap before each of its tokens, summed. */ fun shares(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>): Map<String, Double> { val share = sortedMapOf<String, Double>() var previous = tokens.lastKey() for ((token, node) in tokens) { share[node] = (share[node] ?: 0.0) + (token - previous).toULong().toDouble() / 18446744073709551616.0 previous = token } return share } /** Six nodes, the same names as the ring demo in the Data models track's first lesson. How even is the ring with 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256 tokens each? */ fun main() { val nodes = listOf("node-A", "node-B", "node-C", "node-D", "node-E", "node-F") println("one token per node:") shares(ring(nodes, 1)).forEach { (node, share) -> println(" %s owns %5.1f%%".format(node, share * 100)) } println("tokens per node smallest share largest share largest / fair (16.7%)") for (t in listOf(1, 4, 16, 64, 256)) { val s = shares(ring(nodes, t)).values println("%15d %13.1f%% %12.1f%% %20.2f".format(t, s.min() * 100, s.max() * 100, s.max() * nodes.size)) } }

try.expect:
one token per node:
  node-A owns  13.6%
  node-B owns  26.1%
  node-C owns   1.6%
  node-D owns   7.9%
  node-E owns  44.0%
  node-F owns   6.8%
tokens per node   smallest share   largest share   largest / fair (16.7%)
              1             1.6%           44.0%                   2.64
              4            12.8%           23.4%                   1.40
             16             9.3%           24.3%                   1.46
             64            15.2%           18.6%                   1.12
            256            16.1%           17.4%                   1.04

You get exactly these numbers: MD5 is the same everywhere. With one token, node-E owns 44.0% and node-C 1.6%, a 27-fold spread. Many tokens pull every node toward 16.7%, but not smoothly: 16 random tokens came out slightly worse than 4. Random placement only evens out with large T, which is the cost Cassandra's token allocator avoids. (The shares differ from the Data models track's demo because the tokens here are the hashes of node-A#0 and so on, not of node-A.)

video.title: Consistent hashing: why adding a node moves few keys

sections.h: A joining node takes keys from the nodes beside its tokens
sections.html:
Adding a node isn't free. Before it can serve its keys, the data for them has to be copied to it from the nodes that held them, while those nodes keep serving traffic. In Dynamo's first production design, bootstrapping a new node during the busy shopping season took almost a day, as the paper reports in section 6.2. So it matters how much moves and who has to send it.

With one token per node, the new node takes one arc from one node. In the demo below, node-E joins four nodes and its token lands inside node-D's long arc. E takes 43,894 of 100,000 keys, every one of them from D. One machine streams 44% of the data set on its own. Lesson 1's hash mod S (N there) would have moved 80,221 keys and shuffled them between all five nodes, so the ring is still far better. But one unlucky token decides who does all the work.

With 16 tokens per node, E's 16 tokens land in 16 places, and each one takes the slice just before it from whoever owned it. In the demo 17,842 keys move: 6,997 from A, 5,576 from B and 5,269 from D. Three machines stream a slice each, in parallel. C happened to lose nothing. The stepper shows both joins.

Leaving runs the same film backward. When a node with 16 tokens dies, each of its arcs falls to the next token clockwise, and those tokens belong to many different nodes. Dynamo's paper says a failed node's load "is evenly dispersed across the remaining available nodes". With one token per node, one neighbour inherits all of it.

The ring isn't the only way to get there. Two designs reach the same goal, about 1/S of the keys moving and all of them to the new node, with no ring at all. Rendezvous hashing (Thaler and Ravishankar, 1996), also called highest random weight, scores every node for each key with hash(key + node) and gives the key to the highest score. A new node wins about 1/S of the keys, taken evenly from every old node, and a node that leaves hands its keys evenly to the rest. The price is S hashes per lookup. Jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach, Google, 2014) is a loop of about five lines that maps a key to a bucket numbered 0 to S - 1, with no table and no tokens. Its catch is the numbering: you can add or remove only the last bucket. That suits numbered shards whose replicas handle failures, and doesn't suit a cache cluster where any node can die. The Try-it runs both next to the ring.

Copies need one more rule. A key is stored on N nodes, the first N clockwise from the key, as the Data models track's first lesson described. With virtual nodes the next few tokens often belong to the same machine, and two copies on one machine protect nothing. So the walk skips any token whose node is already on the list, until it has N distinct physical nodes. Dynamo builds its preference list that way (section 4.3), and the lab's preferenceList does too.

frames.say: Copies with virtual nodes. The key sits at the dot; walk clockwise. The first token is B's, so B holds copy 1. The next token is B's again, and two copies on one machine protect nothing, so skip it. Then A, then E. Dynamo builds its preference list this way, skipping positions until it has N distinct physical nodes, and so does the lab.

try.title: Count what moves when node-E joins
steps: Read RingJoinDemo.kt. It places 100,000 payment keys on four nodes, adds node-E, and counts the keys whose owner changed and who gave them up. It does this for hash mod S, for a ring with one token per node and with 16, and for jump hash and rendezvous hashing.
Predict which one moves the most keys, and which ones take keys from all four old nodes.

code.title: RingJoinDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l02.demo /** Jump consistent hash (Lamping and Veach, 2014): a key's bucket from 0 until [buckets], with no table at all. */ fun jumpHash(key: Long, buckets: Int): Int { var k = key var b = -1L var j = 0L while (j < buckets) { b = j k = k * 2862933555777941757L + 1 // a 64-bit linear congruential step: a new pseudo-random k j = ((b + 1) * ((1L shl 31).toDouble() / ((k ushr 33) + 1).toDouble())).toLong() // the next bucket this key jumps to } return b.toInt() } /** Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing: score every node for this key and take the highest. */ fun rendezvous(key: String, nodes: List<String>): String = nodes.maxBy { position("$key|$it") } /** A fifth node joins four. Which keys move, and where do they come from? */ fun main() { val four = listOf("node-A", "node-B", "node-C", "node-D") val five = four + "node-E" val keys = (0 until 100_000).map { "pay-$it" } // lesson 1's placement: node number hash mod S fun modOwner(key: String, nodes: List<String>) = nodes[Math.floorMod(position(key), nodes.size.toLong()).toInt()] val modMoved = keys.count { modOwner(it, four) != modOwner(it, five) } println("hash mod S, 4 -> 5 nodes: %,d of %,d keys move".format(modMoved, keys.size)) for (t in listOf(1, 16)) { val before = ring(four, t) val after = ring(five, t) // the owner is the node of the first token at or after the key; past the top, wrap to the first fun owner(tokens: java.util.TreeMap<Long, String>, key: String) = (tokens.ceilingEntry(position(key)) ?: tokens.firstEntry()).value val moved = keys.filter { owner(before, it) != owner(after, it) } val gaveUp = moved.groupingBy { owner(before, it) }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("ring, %2d token(s) per node: %,d keys move, all to node-E; given up by %s".format(t, moved.size, gaveUp)) } // no ring: jump hash numbers the nodes 0 to 4, rendezvous scores all of them val jumpMoved = keys.filter { jumpHash(position(it), 4) != jumpHash(position(it), 5) } val jumpGaveUp = jumpMoved.groupingBy { four[jumpHash(position(it), 4)] }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("jump hash: %,d keys move, all to node-E; given up by %s".format(jumpMoved.size, jumpGaveUp)) val hrwMoved = keys.filter { rendezvous(it, four) != rendezvous(it, five) } val hrwGaveUp = hrwMoved.groupingBy { rendezvous(it, four) }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("rendezvous: %,d keys move, all to node-E; given up by %s".format(hrwMoved.size, hrwGaveUp)) }

hash mod S, 4 -> 5 nodes: 80,221 of 100,000 keys move
ring,  1 token(s) per node: 43,894 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-D=43894}
ring, 16 token(s) per node: 17,842 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-A=6997, node-B=5576, node-D=5269}
jump hash:               19,792 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-A=4991, node-B=5019, node-C=4895, node-D=4887}
rendezvous:              19,897 keys move, all to node-E; given up by {node-A=5051, node-B=4880, node-C=4967, node-D=4999}

hash mod S reshuffles 80% of the keys between every pair of nodes. On the ring, every key that moves goes to node-E and nobody else trades. With one token, all 43,894 come from node-D, whose arc node-E landed in. With 16 tokens node-E takes about a fifth of the ring (17.8%), from three different nodes; node-C happened to give nothing. Jump hash and rendezvous both move almost exactly the fair fifth, about 5,000 keys from each old node, with no tokens at all.

sections.h: Cassandra: Murmur3 tokens, sixteen per node
sections.html:
Cassandra's ring is every 64-bit number, from -2^63 to 2^63 - 1. Each node's cassandra.yaml names the hash that puts partition keys on it: partitioner: org.apache.cassandra.dht.Murmur3Partitioner. Murmur3 is a fast hash that isn't meant for security, only for spreading. CQL shows you the result: SELECT token(account_id) turns A-1001 into -4994511478997274402. Every cluster in the world computes the same number, because the token depends only on the key.

How many tokens does a node get? The cassandra.yaml in the cassandra:5.0.9 image says num_tokens: 16 and allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3. The Cassandra docs tell the history. Version 2.x picked tokens at random, so it needed 256 per node to even things out. Version 3.x added a token allocator that picks a joining node's tokens on purpose, to balance load for a given replication factor (RF, the number of copies of each row, the N of the Replication track's leaderless lesson), so far fewer tokens do the job. Fewer is better for its own reasons: the docs say each token adds up to 2 × (RF - 1) neighbours on the ring, and cluster-wide maintenance slows down as tokens multiply. Repair, which compares replicas range by range (the Replication track's lesson on leaderless replication), is the main example.

Fewer tokens also fail better. Cassandra 4.0 cut the default from 256 to 16 (CASSANDRA-13701), and The Last Pickle measured why on a six-node cluster with three copies of every row, read at LOCAL_QUORUM, so two of each row's three replicas must answer. They stopped the same two nodes in each test. With one token per node, all the data could still be read. With three tokens per node, 33.3% of it couldn't. Every token range has its own set of three replicas, found by the walk below. With few ranges per node, a node shares ranges with only a few neighbours, and two dead nodes that aren't neighbours share no range. With many ranges per node, almost every pair of nodes shares some range, so losing any two nodes takes some rows below quorum. More tokens even out the load and raise the odds that a double failure makes data unreadable.

Replicas come from the same walk as in the stepper. With replication factor 3, the first copy goes to the node owning the first token at or after the key's token, and the next copies to the next distinct nodes clockwise. NetworkTopologyStrategy, the strategy the docs say every production cluster should use, also spreads the copies across racks and lets each datacenter have its own factor.

The Try-it reads this off a real three-node cluster. A-1001's token falls just before one of cass3's tokens, so cass3 holds the first copy. The next token clockwise is cass1's, the one after that is cass3's again and gets skipped, and the next is cass2's. nodetool getendpoints prints the same three nodes in the same order.

Not every store shows you its tokens. DynamoDB hashes the partition key too, but it decides partition boundaries itself. It splits a partition that grows too large, and, in what its 2022 paper calls split for consumption, one that gets too busy, choosing the split point from the keys it has seen used. Bigtable and HBase don't hash at all. They keep keys in order and split ranges by size, as lesson 1 showed, which keeps range scans cheap and sends every time-ordered insert to the last range.

try.title: Find A-1001's replicas on a three-node ring
steps: From the labs folder, start the three-node cluster: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml up -d --wait. It starts one node at a time and takes about 3 to 4 minutes. It needs about 3 GB of Docker memory.

Load a small table with three copies of every row: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 cqlsh -f /sfz/nosql-06-balances.cql. Find each node's address with docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 hostname -i (then cass2, cass3).
Print the ring: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool ring. Count the lines per address.

Get the tokens of the rows: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 cqlsh -e "SELECT account_id, token(account_id) FROM payments.balances;". Find A-1001's token in the ring printout and write down the three nodes you expect to hold it.

Check: docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml exec cass1 nodetool getendpoints payments balances A-1001. Stop it when you're done with docker compose -f env/cassandra-cluster.yml down -v. Lessons 5 and 6 start it again.

sections.h: The ring spreads keys, not requests: hot keys
sections.html:
It's 12:00 on Black Friday, and merchant M-0042 takes 4,000 payments a second, a fifth of all traffic. The Data models track's single-table design lesson gave the payments table a byMerchant index, a GSI with merchantId as its partition key, so all 4,000 index writes a second carry the same partition key. Everything with one partition key lives in one partition, and the AWS docs cap a partition at 1,000 write units a second, which is 1,000 writes of items up to 1 KB. About 3,000 of those writes a second are throttled, whatever capacity the table has.

Virtual nodes don't help. They balance keys across nodes, and this is one key. Splitting doesn't help either: the 2022 DynamoDB paper says a partition getting high traffic on a single item, or whose key range is written in order, won't benefit from a split. The Dynamo paper assumed this problem away. Its section 6.2 counts on there being "enough keys in the popular end of the distribution". A Black Friday merchant is one key.

So first detect hot keys. Count requests per partition key per second and compare each count with the per-partition limit; the lab builds that detector. In production you don't write it yourself. CloudWatch Contributor Insights for DynamoDB reports the most accessed and the most throttled keys of a table or a GSI, and Cassandra's nodetool toppartitions samples the busiest partitions on a node.

Then spread a write-hot key over several keys. That's write sharding: write M-0042's payments under MERCH#M-0042#0 to MERCH#M-0042#9, choosing the suffix from the payment. The AWS docs describe two ways. A random suffix spreads best, but nobody can find one payment's shard again. A suffix calculated from something you know, here hash(paymentId) mod 10, spreads almost as well and can be computed again for a lookup. Pick the count from numbers: 4,000 writes a second over 1,000 per partition needs at least 4 shards. Ten leaves room for a bigger peak. The demo below gets a busiest shard of 454 writes.

The bill moves to the read side. AP3 from that lesson, "M-0042's FAILED payments since 09:00", is now 10 Queries, one per shard, and your code merges them by time. That's a scatter-gather read, and it's the price of the write fix. Pay it only for keys that are really hot.

A read-hot key is a different problem with a different fix. If every authorization reads M-0042's settings item, that one item is capped at 3,000 read units a second. Eventually consistent reads cost half, so that's 6,000 small reads. Beyond that, cache it: DynamoDB Accelerator, or Redis from the Caching track, and don't shard it.

try.title: Watch one merchant overload one node, then shard it
steps: Read HotKeyDemo.kt. It puts six nodes on a well-balanced ring (256 tokens each), then sends one second of Black Friday writes: 20,000 payments over 2,000 merchants, with M-0042 taking 4,000. It counts writes per node and per key, first keyed by merchant, then with a shard suffix from the payment id.
Predict the busiest node's count in each case, and the busiest key's.

code.title: HotKeyDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.shard.l02.demo /** Black Friday: one merchant takes a fifth of all payments. Spread the KEYS evenly, and see what happens to the LOAD. */ fun main() { val nodes = (1..6).map { "node-$it" } val tokens = ring(nodes, 256) // a well-balanced ring: every node owns close to 1/6 fun owner(key: String) = (tokens.ceilingEntry(position(key)) ?: tokens.firstEntry()).value // one second of writes: 20,000 payments over 2,000 merchants, but M-0042 takes 4,000 of them val payments = (0 until 20_000).map { i -> (if (i % 5 == 0) "M-0042" else "M-%04d".format(1_000 + i % 1_999)) to "pay-$i" } fun report(title: String, keyOf: (String, String) -> String) { val perKey = payments.groupingBy { (m, p) -> keyOf(m, p) }.eachCount() val perNode = payments.groupingBy { (m, p) -> owner(keyOf(m, p)) }.eachCount().toSortedMap() val hottest = perKey.maxBy { it.value } println(title) println(" writes per node: $perNode") println(" busiest key: ${hottest.key} with ${hottest.value} writes; keys over 1,000: ${perKey.count { it.value > 1_000 }}") } report("partition key MERCH#<merchant>:") { m, _ -> "MERCH#$m" } // write sharding: a suffix calculated from the payment id, 0 to 9 report("partition key MERCH#<merchant>#<shard of 10>:") { m, p -> "MERCH#$m#${Math.floorMod(position(p), 10L)}" } }

try.expect:
partition key MERCH#<merchant>:
  writes per node: {node-1=2553, node-2=2778, node-3=6777, node-4=2489, node-5=2906, node-6=2497}
  busiest key: MERCH#M-0042 with 4000 writes; keys over 1,000: 1
partition key MERCH#<merchant>#<shard of 10>:
  writes per node: {node-1=3557, node-2=2712, node-3=3206, node-4=2828, node-5=2821, node-6=4876}
  busiest key: MERCH#M-0042#5 with 454 writes; keys over 1,000: 0

The ring is nearly perfect, and node-3 still takes 6,777 writes while the others take about 2,500, because one key can't be split across nodes. After sharding no key is over 1,000. The nodes are more even but not perfectly so: ten shards land on six nodes, and node-6 drew more than its share of them. The per-key limit is the one that throttles, and it's fixed.

refs.title: Using write sharding to distribute workloads evenly (DynamoDB Developer Guide)
CloudWatch Contributor Insights for DynamoDB: how it works

analogy: Picture a round table where every guest serves the dishes that land between them and the guest on their left. Seat six guests at random and one ends up with a huge stretch of table while another has a sliver. Give every guest sixteen raffle tickets placed round the table instead, each ticket covering the stretch before it, and every guest ends up with about a sixth. A new guest who arrives takes a few small stretches from several neighbours instead of half of one person's. The analogy breaks on hot keys: if everyone at the party orders the same dish, the tickets don't matter, because that one dish sits in one spot and only the guest whose stretch it's in can serve it. You have to cook it in ten pots on ten spots of the table.
world: Kafka has already taught you the hot-key problem under another name. Partition a payments topic by merchant id and M-0042's Black Friday traffic lands on one partition, one broker and one consumer thread, while the other consumers wait. The fixes are the same as here: a better key, or a key with a suffix plus a merge on the read side. In DynamoDB, turn on Contributor Insights for the throttled-keys mode on the payments table and every GSI before peak season; it costs little when nothing is throttled. Size write shards from your own numbers: last year's peak payments per second for your biggest merchant, divided by 1,000. And keep merchant settings that every authorization reads in a cache in front of the store, not in a hot item.
mistake: The most common mistake is believing that a good hash or a big cluster protects you from hot spots. People see the ring spread a million account ids evenly and assume any key design will be spread too. Then a partition key with few values (a merchant id, a status, today's date) takes a big share of the traffic, and throttling starts on one partition while the table's metrics say it's mostly idle. The fix is to check the key design against the traffic, not against the key count. Find the busiest value of every partition key, table and indexes, at peak, compare it with 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads a second, and shard or cache the ones that come close.

  M-0042 ->  5210081981202411406

scan A-1000 .. A-1999   -> every node; no order between partitions
order exists only inside one partition, by the sort key

compare.note: Range partitioning keeps neighbours together, so a range scan is cheap, and it splits a range when it grows. Its weak spot is any key that grows with time: every insert lands at the end. Hash partitioning scatters neighbouring keys on purpose, so writes spread whatever their keys look like, but a scan across partitions has to ask every node. Cassandra and DynamoDB take both: hash the partition key to choose the place, then keep rows sorted inside it. Neither one protects you from a single hot key.

worked.title: Shard M-0042's merchant index for Black Friday

steps.say: Start from numbers, not from a guess. Last year's peak for M-0042 was 4,000 payments a second. Each index item is about 600 bytes, so each write costs 1 write unit. One partition takes 1,000 a second.
steps.code:
peak writes        4,000 / s     (M-0042 at 12:00 on Black Friday)
write units each   1             (600-byte item, rounded up to 1 KB)
per partition      1,000 / s
minimum shards     4,000 / 1,000 = 4
chosen             10            (room for 2.5x last year's peak)

steps.say: On the write path, give every payment a shard number calculated from its payment id, so the same payment always lands on the same shard and a lookup can compute it again. With a multi-attribute GSI key, a new merchant index takes (merchantId, shard) as its partition key; with a one-attribute key you'd write MERCH#M-0042#3 into a single attribute, as the lab does.
steps.code: fun shardOf(paymentId: String): Int = // the same id always gives the same shard; ids spread evenly over 0..9 Math.floorMod(HashRing.position(paymentId), 10L).toInt() // the payment item from the Data models track's single-table lesson, plus the attribute the sharded index is keyed on val item = Keys.paymentItem(p) + mapOf("shard" to Keys.n(shardOf(p.paymentId).toLong()))

steps.say: On the read path, AP3 becomes a scatter-gather: one Query per shard, run in parallel, then a merge by time. Each shard is asked for the full page size, because the newest 50 could all sit on one shard.
steps.code: suspend fun failedPayments(merchantId: String, from: Instant, limit: Int): List<Payment> = coroutineScope { (0 until 10) .map { shard -> async(Dispatchers.IO) { queryShard(merchantId, shard, "FAILED", from, limit) } } .awaitAll() // 10 Queries in flight at once .flatten() .sortedByDescending { it.createdAt } // merge: newest first across shards .take(limit) }

steps.say: Check the bill against the win. Writes now spread over ten partition keys. Reads of AP3 cost ten requests instead of one, and up to ten times the items. That's the right trade for M-0042 at peak and the wrong one for the 1,999 merchants who never come near 1,000 a second, so shard only the keys your numbers say are hot.
steps.code:
one key          10 shards
busiest key at peak    4,000 / s        about 450 / s
throttled writes       about 3,000 / s  none
AP3 requests           1                10, in parallel
AP3 items read         limit            up to 10 x limit

lab.title: Build a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes, then catch a hot key
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker needed. Twelve of thirteen fail with NotImplementedError; the one about hash mod S uses the given modOwner and passes.

In HashRing.kt, write addNode (one loop) and ownerOf (one TreeMap lookup, plus the wrap). The tests on ownership, joining and removing pass: watch the one that checks a joining node takes keys from one neighbour with one token and from several with sixteen.
Write preferenceList: walk the tokens clockwise from the key's position, wrapping once, and keep distinct nodes until you have n. The test compares you with a slow walk over every token.
In HotKeys.kt, write HotKeyDetector.record and hotKeys, then WriteSharding.shardKey. All thirteen pass.
Experiment: in the last test of HotKeysTest, change the shard count from 10 to 3 and run it again. 4,000 writes over 3 keys is still more than 1,000 per key, and the test says so. Put it back.
hints: tokens.ceilingEntry(position(key)) is the first token at or after the key, or null past the top of the ring. ?: tokens.firstEntry() wraps around.

For the walk, tokens.tailMap(position(key), true).values is the rest of the ring clockwise, and tokens.values is the whole ring from the bottom. Chain the two as sequences and stop as soon as you have enough. A LinkedHashSet keeps order and ignores duplicates.
Ask for n copies on a ring of 2 nodes and you can only get 2: stop at minOf(n, nodes.size).
The second of a timestamp is Math.floorDiv(atMillis, 1000L). HashMap.merge(key, 1, Int::plus) counts, and merge(key, n, ::maxOf) keeps a maximum.
Positions are signed, so position(paymentId) % 10 can be negative. Math.floorMod can't.
lab.done: All thirteen tests in HashRingTest and HotKeysTest pass.

drill.title: The ring lookup and the replica walk from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a Kotlin function owner(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long): String and a function replicas(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long, n: Int): List<String> that returns n distinct nodes clockwise from the key. Then say in one sentence why replicas has to skip some tokens.

answer.html: fun owner(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long): String = // the first token at or after the key; past the top of the ring, wrap to the first token (tokens.ceilingEntry(keyPosition) ?: tokens.firstEntry()).value fun replicas(tokens: TreeMap<Long, String>, keyPosition: Long, n: Int): List<String> { val want = minOf(n, tokens.values.toSet().size) val found = LinkedHashSet<String>() // clockwise from the key to the top, then from the bottom: each token at most once for (node in tokens.tailMap(keyPosition, true).values.asSequence() + tokens.values.asSequence()) { found += node if (found.size == want) break } return found.toList() } // With virtual nodes, the next tokens often belong to a node already on the list, // and two copies on one machine are lost together when it dies.

recap: With one random token per node, shares are very uneven: about 41% for the luckiest of six nodes against a fair 16.7%.

Virtual nodes give each node many tokens; its share is a sum of small arcs and lands near the average. Random tokens need many per node, which is why Cassandra 5.0 pairs num_tokens: 16 with a token allocator.

A joining node takes the slice before each of its tokens; with many tokens it takes small slices from several nodes, and a failed node's load spreads the same way. Replica walks skip tokens of nodes already chosen.

Rendezvous hashing (score every node, take the highest) and jump hash (no memory, buckets numbered 0 to S - 1) also move only the new node's share, without a ring. More tokens per node balance load but make a double failure more likely to take some range below quorum.
Cassandra hashes the partition key with Murmur3 to a 64-bit token; token() in CQL and nodetool getendpoints show where a row lives.

The ring balances keys, not requests. One hot partition key is capped at 1,000 writes and 3,000 reads a second in DynamoDB. Detect it per key, then shard writes with a calculated suffix and merge on read, or cache hot reads.

explain.prompt: A teammate is sizing a six-node Cassandra cluster and asks: why do we need 16 tokens per node instead of one, and will that also save us when M-0042 does 4,000 payments a second on Black Friday? Answer both.
explain.answer: With one token per node, each node owns the single arc that ends at its token, and six random points cut a circle very unevenly: the luckiest node owns about 41% of the ring on average, so it stores and serves about 41% of everything. When a node joins, it takes its whole share from one neighbour, and when one dies, one neighbour inherits all of its load. With many tokens per node, each node owns many small arcs, the shares even out, a joining node takes small slices from several nodes in parallel, and a dead node's load spreads over many. Cassandra 5.0 uses 16 tokens and an allocator that places them deliberately for replication factor 3, because random tokens need hundreds per node to even out and every token makes repair and streaming slower. None of that helps M-0042. Tokens balance keys, and M-0042's payments share one partition key, so they all hit one partition and its replicas. For that we shard the key, for example merchant id plus a suffix from 0 to 9 calculated from the payment id, and the merchant dashboard merges the ten partitions on read.

deeper.html:
Dynamo's paper, section 6.2, tells how Amazon changed its partitioning scheme in production, and the three strategies are a good map of the design space.

Strategy Tokens Partitions Problem it had or fixed
1 T random tokens per node ranges between tokens bootstrapping took almost a day; Merkle trees had to be rebuilt whenever ranges changed
2 T random tokens per node Q equal-sized ranges separated placement from partitioning; the worst balance, used only during the migration
3 Q/S tokens per node Q equal-sized ranges the best balance in their measurements; a partition moves as one file, so bootstrapping and archiving got simpler

Strategy 3's price, in the paper's words, is that changing the membership needs coordination to keep the assignment right. Cassandra's token allocator works on the same problem from the other side: it keeps the number of tokens per node fixed and chooses where the new ones go.

The 2022 DynamoDB paper tells the other half: how the service learned to live with hot partitions. At first each partition got a fixed share of the table's provisioned throughput, and splitting a partition for size divided that share, so a table could be throttled while mostly idle. DynamoDB added bursting (unused capacity saved for up to 300 seconds), then adaptive capacity (boosting the partitions that were being throttled), and then replaced both with global admission control, which tracks a table's consumption across all request routers with token buckets. Split for consumption came on top: a partition that gets too busy is split at a point chosen from the keys it has seen. The paper's own limit is the one this lesson ends on: a single hot item, or a key range written in order, can't be helped by a split.

If you want to see the 2 × (RF - 1) neighbours rule, look at the token ranges a node is responsible for with nodetool describering payments on the three-node cluster. With 16 tokens per node, each node streams and repairs dozens of ranges instead of three.
